On Christmas Eve, to mark the first anniversary of the Hong Kong armistice, the streets were hung all over with the flags of Japan and its war ensigns, and geisha in kimono had taken the place of the white-bearded Father Christmas. Everywhere were Japanese soldiers making free with their pleasures.

Zuo Qiuming came on foot to the King's Hotel on Lockhart Road, and the moment he stepped into the lobby he saw that the place was blown. He did not leave. Instead he went straight to the telephone booth, swallowed a slip of paper, dialed a number, and hung up without waiting for an answer. He drew a pistol from inside his coat, worked the bolt, dropped it into his overcoat pocket, and, gripping it there, pushed the door open and came out.

That was when the plainclothesmen closed in. Zuo Qiuming drew and shot two of them down, ran behind a pillar, and set the pistol to his own temple. But before he could pull the trigger a bullet caught him in the chest, and he pitched to the ground.

An hour later, while Suzuki Masao was operating, the door of the room was shoved roughly open. In came a Japanese army lieutenant in full uniform. He flashed a Tokkō credential, bowed to the surgeon, and said, in Japanese, "Be so good as to open his belly. What we want will have gone down into his stomach."
Suzuki Masao signaled the nurse to take off his mask, and spread his hands. "That would take his life."
"His life is not important," the lieutenant said. "The intelligence is."
"But I'm a doctor," Suzuki Masao said. "I can't do this."
"You are first a soldier of the Empire," the lieutenant said. "You will obey orders."
Suzuki Masao stood a moment, head bowed, then went to the table and took the scalpel from the nurse's hand.
The lieutenant was losing patience. He stepped up and threw back the sheet over Zuo Qiuming. "Be quick, if you please."
Suzuki Masao paid him no heed. He had the nurse put another dose of anesthetic into Zuo Qiuming's vein, and only then opened the belly with a single stroke.

Two days later Zuo Qiuming came, against all odds, back to life. And then he chose to end it himself. Deep in the night of the third day, when the doctors and nurses had finished their rounds and gone, he pulled off the oxygen mask, drew the drip from his vein, worked both hands under the quilt, and tore open the two wounds on his body. Then, eyes open, he lay still in the dark and let the blood go, drop by drop, through the searing pain.
They sat in the hall of a teahouse, and Suzuki Masao told Lin Nansheng all of it. When he had finished he rose, made a deep and solemn bow, then sat down again. "Pang-san, I've failed your friend."
Lin Nansheng said nothing. Only when he had drunk the scalding tea to the last did he set the cup down. "You're mistaken. He was not my friend."
"I saw him come to visit you. More than once."
"Talk like that could get me arrested."
"I'm your doctor, and your friend as well." Suzuki Masao said it in earnest. "I asked you out only to tell you this: a brave man deserves an honorable grave, not a slab in the mortuary."
Lin Nansheng said, calmly, "Suzuki, to pity your enemy is to betray your Empire."
"I have no enemies." Suzuki Masao looked up at Lin Nansheng. "As a doctor, I have only patients."

Not a trace of it showed on Lin Nansheng's face. He only went on drinking his tea and filling the cup, and when he left the teahouse he went back to the office, to his coming and going as before. He took the meeting with Suzuki Masao for some kind of Japanese probe. Then, a few days later, he saw in the paper the notice calling for someone to claim an unnamed man's body. Looking at the likeness of Zuo Qiuming in the photograph, Lin Nansheng felt his heart rise and fall.
That night he sought out the Juntong's senior officer in Hong Kong. When he had said his piece, the officer opened a drawer and took out a sheaf of files. "You're the analyst. You judge."

The files were full of photographs: the places Zuo Qiuming had gone, the people he had met. On one of them Lin Nansheng saw Ji Zhongyuan's profile, and understood at once. Still he said, "What does this prove?"
"That's why we still have to sift it. This is the last chance."
"He's a dead man already."
"But we have to know whose martyr he is." The officer heaved a long sigh, stood, and gave a globe a hard spin. "If I've not judged wrong, someone will come to claim the body."

Lin Nansheng said not another word. He left the office, went to the bars on Queen's Road, and drank without stopping, trading jokes without stopping with the bar girls; then, half a bottle in hand, he came drunk to the mouth of the lane where he had met Ji Zhongyuan, and, like a man with no home to go to, lay drunk there five deep nights running.

Deep in the night of the sixth day a pedicab circled once and stopped in front of him. Ji Zhongyuan, dressed as its driver, helped him aboard. Lin Nansheng let out a long breath. "So you've shown yourself at last."
Pedaling hard, Ji Zhongyuan said, "And if I hadn't?"
Lin Nansheng asked back, "Would you have given it up?"
As the sky began to pale, Ji Zhongyuan took him across the water to a burial ground on Lantau Island. They stood before a new grave with no stone. "I know the two of you were friends of many years."
"When did he start working for you?"
"He worked for no one," Ji Zhongyuan said. "He was only doing a Chinese agent's duty."

Lin Nansheng stood a while, head bowed, then went back to the boat and said not a word the whole way, sitting alone at the bow into the rising sun and the sea wind. Only ashore did he turn to Ji Zhongyuan. "Put the traffic together and it's plain: the Japanese army will soon move on Guangzhouwan."
"And the French forces?"

"The British couldn't even hold Hong Kong. Can the French?" With that Lin Nansheng turned to go. But a few steps on he came back, looked at Ji Zhongyuan, and hesitated. "I hope your people in Shanghai can help find out what became of her..."
"Rest easy." Ji Zhongyuan cut him off, his face without expression. "She's our comrade, and my wife."

To take in the intelligence Lin Nansheng sent over, Ji Zhongyuan opened a special line and received it himself. But those days did not last long. All at once a transfer order came, and Lin Nansheng was recalled to Chongqing to take up a post as a technical instructor at the Sino-American Cooperative Organization.

Before he left, Lin Nansheng said goodbye to no one, nor did he reach out to Ji Zhongyuan; alone and downcast he came to the pier and boarded the liner behind the other passengers. But the instant he stepped into the cabin, the first thing he saw was Ji Zhongyuan. In the white uniform of a steward, a tray of hot towels in his hands, Ji came up smiling. "Wipe your face, sir."
Lin Nansheng said, coldly, "Do you mean to see me all the way to Chongqing?"
Still smiling, Ji Zhongyuan handed him the towel, and with it a slip of paper. "Whenever you need to reach us, run this in the Central Daily News."
On the slip was a seven-character regulated poem, 'Ode to the Plum Blossom,' signed: Huang Shanyun.
Leaning on the rail, Lin Nansheng read it through once in silence, then tore it to shreds and let them fall into the sea. He shut his eyes, and heard the steam whistle blow.
